notes.definition: Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which uses information from temperature receptors to trigger responses in blood vessels, sweat glands and skeletal muscles that keep the core temperature close to 37 °C.
explanation: Human core body temperature is kept at about 37 °C, the optimum temperature for the enzymes in our cells. It is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain. This centre contains receptors that are sensitive to the temperature of the blood flowing through it. The skin also contains temperature receptors, which send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre, giving early warning of changes in the external temperature.

If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries dilate (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface of the skin. Sweat is also produced by the sweat glands. Both of these responses cause more energy to be transferred from the skin to the environment, so body temperature falls.

If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries constrict (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface of the skin. Sweating stops. Skeletal muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly, which is called shivering. These responses reduce energy transfer to the environment and release extra energy within the body, so body temperature rises.

These responses are automatic. The effectors are the muscles in the walls of blood vessels, the sweat glands and the skeletal muscles. Notice that blood vessels do not move up or down in the skin: they change in width, which changes how much blood flows through the capillaries near the surface.

Higher tier students must be able to explain how each mechanism raises or lowers temperature in a given context. Vasodilation lets more warm blood flow close to the skin surface, so more energy is transferred to the surroundings by radiation. Sweat evaporating from the skin transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings. Vasoconstriction reduces the flow of warm blood near the surface, reducing energy transfer. Shivering needs energy from respiration, and respiration transfers some energy as heat, warming the blood.
keyFacts: Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain.
The thermoregulatory centre contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood.
Skin temperature receptors send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.
Too hot: blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced.
Vasodilation and sweating transfer more energy from the skin to the environment.
Too cold: blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction), sweating stops and skeletal muscles contract (shivering).
Effectors include sweat glands, muscles in blood vessel walls and skeletal muscles.
Shivering raises temperature because muscle contraction requires respiration, which releases energy.
Blood vessels change width; they do not move closer to or further from the skin surface.

keyTerms.definition: The part of the brain that monitors and controls body temperature.
Widening of the blood vessels that supply skin capillaries, so more blood flows near the skin surface.
Narrowing of the blood vessels that supply skin capillaries, so less blood flows near the skin surface.
A gland in the skin that produces sweat; evaporation of sweat transfers energy away from the skin.
Rapid, repeated contraction of skeletal muscles that releases extra energy from respiration.
The temperature deep inside the body, kept at about 37 °C in humans.

workedExamples.title: Responding to a hot environment
workedExamples.question: Describe the responses that occur when a person's body temperature rises above normal on a hot day.
steps: The rise is detected by receptors in the thermoregulatory centre (blood temperature) and by temperature receptors in the skin, which send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.
The thermoregulatory centre causes blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries to dilate (vasodilation).
Both responses transfer more energy from the skin to the environment, so body temperature falls.
workedExamples.answer: Vasodilation and sweating increase energy transfer from the skin to the surroundings, lowering body temperature.

workedExamples.title: Explaining shivering (Higher)
workedExamples.question: A swimmer in cold water starts to shiver. Explain how shivering helps to raise body temperature.
steps: Shivering is rapid contraction of skeletal muscles.
Muscle contraction needs energy, so the rate of respiration in muscle cells increases.
Respiration transfers some energy as heat (it is exothermic).
This warms the blood, so body temperature rises.
workedExamples.answer: Shivering increases respiration in skeletal muscles; respiration releases energy as heat, which raises body temperature.

workedExamples.question: In a cold room, the blood flow to a person's hand fell from 400 cm³/min to 60 cm³/min. Calculate the percentage decrease.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when we are hot.
misconceptions.right: In fact blood vessels do not move. Vessels supplying the skin capillaries widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows through capillaries near the surface.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that sweating cools you because the sweat is cold.
misconceptions.right: In fact sweat cools you when it evaporates, because evaporation transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think capillaries dilate or constrict.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the blood vessels supplying the capillaries (arterioles), which have muscle in their walls, that dilate or constrict. Capillaries have no muscle.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think shivering produces "heat energy" from nowhere.
misconceptions.right: In fact shivering increases respiration in muscles, and respiration transfers some energy by heating.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the skin is the coordination centre for temperature control.
misconceptions.right: In fact the skin contains receptors; the thermoregulatory centre in the brain is the coordination centre.

realWorld: Hypothermia: if core temperature falls below about 35 °C, enzymes slow down and the person can become confused and lose consciousness, so walkers and swimmers in cold conditions are warned to wear insulating clothing.
Heat stroke can occur in very hot, humid weather when sweat cannot evaporate quickly enough, so athletes are advised to drink plenty of water and rest in shade.
Foil blankets are given to marathon runners after a race to reduce energy transfer from their skin as their body cools.
Fans help to cool people because moving air increases the rate at which sweat evaporates.
higherTier: Explain how each mechanism raises or lowers body temperature in a given context.
Vasodilation: more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface, so more energy is transferred to the surroundings by radiation.
Sweating: water in sweat evaporates from the skin, transferring energy from the skin to the surroundings.
Vasoconstriction: less blood flows near the skin surface, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Shivering: muscle contraction needs respiration, which releases energy and warms the blood.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology (8461) only, not in Combined Science Trilogy.
The thermoregulatory centre, skin temperature receptors, vasodilation, sweating, vasoconstriction and shivering.
examTips: Spell and use "vasodilation" and "vasoconstriction" correctly, and say it is the blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries that change width.
Never write that blood vessels "move". Examiners will not give the mark.
For Higher marks, explain how each response changes energy transfer: more or less energy transferred from the skin to the environment.
Say sweat cools the body when it evaporates, not just that sweat is produced.
Use "thermoregulatory centre in the brain" rather than just "the brain" when you can.
summary: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors and controls body temperature.
It has receptors for blood temperature and receives impulses from skin temperature receptors.
Too hot: vasodilation and sweating transfer more energy to the environment.
Too cold: vasoconstriction, sweating stops and shivering.
Higher: explain each mechanism in terms of energy transfer and respiration.

questions.question: Where is the thermoregulatory centre found?
markScheme: 1 mark: in the brain
questions.explanation: The thermoregulatory centre is in the brain. The skin contains temperature receptors that send impulses to it.

questions.question: What does the thermoregulatory centre contain that allows it to monitor body temperature?
options: Receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood
markScheme: 1 mark: receptors sensitive to blood temperature
questions.explanation: The thermoregulatory centre contains receptors that detect the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.

questions.question: What happens to the blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries when the body is too hot?
options: They move closer to the skin surface
markScheme: 1 mark: they dilate (vasodilation)
questions.explanation: When too hot, blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate, so more blood flows near the surface. They do not move.

questions.question: Which of these is a response to the body being too cold?
markScheme: 1 mark: shivering
questions.explanation: When too cold, skeletal muscles contract (shiver), sweating stops and blood vessels constrict. Sweating and vasodilation are responses to being too hot.

questions.question: What is vasoconstriction?
options: Production of sweat by sweat glands
Widening of blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries
Narrowing of blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries
markScheme: 1 mark: narrowing of blood vessels supplying skin capillaries
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface, reducing energy transfer to the environment.

questions.question: How do temperature receptors in the skin send information to the thermoregulatory centre?
options: By changing the temperature of the blood only
markScheme: 1 mark: by nervous impulses
questions.explanation: The skin contains temperature receptors that send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.

questions.question: Which effectors contract during shivering?
options: Muscles in the walls of the stomach
markScheme: 1 mark: skeletal muscles
questions.explanation: Shivering is the rapid contraction of skeletal muscles.

questions.question: Which statement explains why sweating lowers body temperature?
options: Sweat is colder than the skin, so it cools the blood
Water in sweat evaporates, transferring energy from the skin to the surroundings
Sweat contains salt, which absorbs energy from the body
Sweating reduces blood flow to the skin
markScheme: 1 mark: evaporation transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings
questions.explanation: It is the evaporation of sweat that transfers energy away from the skin. Sweat is produced at body temperature, so it is not "cold".

questions.question: Which statement explains how vasoconstriction helps to raise body temperature?
options: Blood vessels move deeper into the skin
More sweat is produced, which insulates the body
Blood flows faster, so it produces more energy
Less blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: less blood near skin surface, so less energy transferred to surroundings
questions.explanation: Narrowing the vessels supplying skin capillaries reduces flow of warm blood near the surface, so less energy is lost. Vessels do not move.

questions.question: How does shivering help to increase body temperature?
options: Muscle contractions need respiration, which releases energy and warms the blood
Shivering stops blood flowing to the skin
Shivering causes the thermoregulatory centre to make heat
markScheme: 1 mark: muscle contraction needs respiration, which releases energy
questions.explanation: Contracting muscles need energy from respiration. Respiration transfers some energy as heat, which raises body temperature.

questions.question: Which pair of responses both happen when body temperature is too high?
markScheme: 1 mark: vasodilation and sweating
questions.explanation: Vasodilation and sweating both increase energy transfer from the skin to the environment.

questions.question: On a hot, humid day, sweating is less effective at cooling the body. What is the best explanation?
options: Less sweat is produced in humid air
Sweat evaporates more slowly because the air already contains a lot of water vapour
The thermoregulatory centre stops working in humid air
markScheme: 1 mark: sweat evaporates more slowly in humid air
questions.explanation: Sweat cools by evaporating. In humid air evaporation is slower, so less energy is transferred from the skin.

questions.question: During an illness, a person's core body temperature rose from 37.0 °C to 38.6 °C. Calculate the increase in temperature.
questions.explanation: Increase = final − initial = 38.6 − 37.0 = 1.6 °C.

questions.question: A runner loses 1.2 dm³ of sweat per hour. Calculate the total volume of sweat lost during a race lasting 2.5 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3.0 dm³
questions.explanation: Total = rate × time = 1.2 × 2.5 = 3.0 dm³. This water must be replaced by drinking.

questions.question: Blood flow to the skin of a person's arm was 250 cm³/min at rest in a cool room and 1750 cm³/min after exercise in a hot room. How many times greater was the blood flow after exercise?
markScheme: 1 mark: 7 (times)
questions.explanation: 1750 ÷ 250 = 7. The large increase is caused by vasodilation of blood vessels supplying skin capillaries.

questions.question: In a cold room, blood flow to a person's hand decreased from 400 cm³/min to 60 cm³/min. Calculate the percentage decrease in blood flow.
markScheme: 1 mark: 85%
questions.explanation: Change = 340 cm³/min; 340 ÷ 400 × 100 = 85%. This is due to vasoconstriction, which reduces energy transfer from the skin.

questions.question: When 1 g of sweat evaporates from the skin, about 2.4 kJ of energy is transferred from the body. Calculate the energy transferred when 500 g of sweat evaporates.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1200 kJ
questions.explanation: Energy = 2.4 kJ/g × 500 g = 1200 kJ. Evaporation of sweat is a very effective way of transferring energy away from the body.

questions.question: Name two responses of the body when its temperature is too high.
markScheme: 1 mark: blood vessels (supplying skin capillaries) dilate / vasodilation
1 mark: sweat produced by sweat glands
questions.explanation: Both responses increase energy transfer from the skin to the environment.

questions.question: Describe three responses of the body when its temperature is too low.
markScheme: 1 mark: blood vessels (supplying skin capillaries) constrict / vasoconstriction
1 mark: sweating stops
1 mark: skeletal muscles contract / shivering
questions.explanation: These are the three AQA responses to a low body temperature.

questions.question: After exercising on a hot day, a person's skin looks red. Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: more blood flows near skin surface
markScheme: 1 mark: blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate / vasodilation
1 mark: more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface
questions.explanation: The red colour comes from the extra blood flowing near the surface of the skin.

questions.question: Describe how the thermoregulatory centre receives information about body temperature.
markScheme: 1 mark: receptors in the thermoregulatory centre detect the temperature of the blood
1 mark: temperature receptors in the skin send nervous impulses to it
questions.explanation: The centre gets information from inside (blood temperature) and outside (skin receptors).

questions.question: Explain how vasodilation helps to lower body temperature.
acceptedAnswers: blood vessels supplying skin capillaries widen
markScheme: 1 mark: blood vessels supplying skin capillaries widen / dilate
1 mark: more (warm) blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface
1 mark: so more energy is transferred from the skin to the environment (by radiation)
questions.explanation: More warm blood close to the surface means more energy can be transferred from the skin to the cooler surroundings.

questions.question: A person who falls into cold water starts to shiver and their skin becomes pale. Explain why their skin becomes pale.
markScheme: 1 mark: vasoconstriction / blood vessels supplying skin capillaries narrow
1 mark: less blood flows near the skin surface (so it looks pale and less energy is transferred to the water)
questions.explanation: Less blood near the surface makes the skin pale and reduces energy transfer to the cold water.

questions.question: Explain why people should drink water when exercising in hot weather.
markScheme: 1 mark: they produce a lot of sweat / lose water by sweating
1 mark: water must be replaced to avoid dehydration (and allow sweating to continue)
questions.explanation: Sweating cools the body but loses water. Drinking replaces this water.

questions.question: Suggest why sitting in front of a fan helps a hot, sweaty person to cool down.
markScheme: 1 mark: moving air increases the rate of evaporation of sweat
1 mark: so more energy is transferred from the skin to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Sweat cools by evaporating. Moving air carries away water vapour, so evaporation is faster.

questions.question: State the normal core body temperature of a human.
markScheme: 1 mark: about 37 °C
questions.explanation: Human core body temperature is kept at about 37 °C, the optimum for enzymes in human cells.

questions.question: Describe how the body responds when its core temperature falls below normal.
markScheme: Indicative content: fall detected by receptors in the thermoregulatory centre (sensitive to blood temperature); skin temperature receptors send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre; thermoregulatory centre in the brain coordinates response; blood vessels supplying skin capillaries constrict (vasoconstriction); less blood flows near the skin surface; less energy transferred to the environment; sweating stops; skeletal muscles contract (shivering); respiration in muscles releases energy; body temperature rises back towards 37 °C.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of detection by receptors and the thermoregulatory centre AND at least two correct responses, with some explanation of their effect.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two responses named with little detail, or detection described without responses.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Good answers include detection (receptors and thermoregulatory centre) and the three responses, and say how each one helps.

questions.question: A marathon runner is running on a hot day. Explain how the runner's body detects and responds to the rise in core body temperature, and how the responses lower body temperature.
markScheme: Indicative content: respiration in muscles during running releases energy, raising body temperature; receptors in the thermoregulatory centre in the brain detect the rise in blood temperature; temperature receptors in the skin send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre; vasodilation: blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate; more warm blood flows near the skin surface; more energy transferred to the environment by radiation; sweat glands produce more sweat; sweat evaporates from the skin; evaporation transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings; on a hot day less energy can be transferred by radiation, so sweating is especially important; runner loses water in sweat so must drink; humid conditions slow evaporation.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logical explanation of detection AND both vasodilation and sweating, each linked clearly to energy transfer from the skin to the environment, applied to the runner.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): detection and responses described with some explanation of how they lower temperature.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): responses named with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: For the highest marks, explain each response in terms of energy transfer and apply it to the context (running increases respiration; hot weather makes sweating the main way to lose energy).
